facts.statement: The genus Saurichthys was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1834.
facts.quote: authority: Agassiz, 1834

facts.statement: Saurichthys was an extinct predatory ray-finned fish that lived during the Triassic Period.
facts.quote: Saurichthys (from , 'lizard' and 'fish') is an extinct genus of predatory ray-finned fish from the Triassic Period.

facts.statement: Fossils of Saurichthys have been discovered on every continent except South America and Antarctica.
facts.quote: Fossils of Saurichthys have been found on all continents except South America and Antarctica.

facts.statement: Saurichthys lived in both marine and freshwater environments.
facts.quote: It inhabited both marine and freshwater environments.

facts.statement: The oldest known fossils of Saurichthys come from the Wordie Creek Formation in East Greenland and date to the Early Triassic (Griesbachian/Induan stage).
facts.quote: The oldest fossils of Saurichthys were recovered from the Wordie Creek Formation in East Greenland and are Griesbachian (Induan, Early Triassic) in age.

facts.statement: More than 50 species of Saurichthys have been described by scientists.
facts.quote: Over 50 species of Saurichthys have been described

facts.statement: Louis Agassiz named the type species Saurichthys "lizard fish" in 1834 because its skeletal features appeared intermediate between reptiles and fishes.
facts.quote: Louis Agassiz, who described the type species of Saurichthys in 1834, named it the "lizard fish" because of skeletal features that he thought were intermediate to reptiles and fishes.

facts.statement: Saurichthys was an elongate, streamlined fish that typically measured between 0.6 and 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: Saurichthys was an elongate, streamlined fish, commonly about 0.6 m to 1 m long.

facts.statement: While some species were only a few decimeters long, others could reach approximately 1.5 meters in length, such as a specimen from the Middle Triassic of Turkey.
facts.quote: Some species were only a few decimetres long (e.g. Saurichthys minimahleri), while others could grow up to about 1.5 m in length (specimen from the Middle Triassic of Turkey).

facts.statement: Saurichthys possessed extremely long jaws that constituted one-third of its total body length and terminated in a sharp, beak-like tip.
facts.quote: Its jaws were extremely long, making up a third of the total body length, and ended in a sharp, beak-like tip.

facts.statement: The dorsal and anal fins of Saurichthys were positioned opposite each other near the rear of the body, and it had a symmetrical, abbreviated diphycercal tail.
facts.quote: Its dorsal and anal fins were placed opposite each other well back on the body, and the tail was symmetrical (abbreviate diphycercal).

facts.statement: Saurichthys is interpreted as an ambush predator, exhibiting behavior similar to modern gars and needlefish.
facts.quote: Saurichthys is classically interpreted as an ambush predator, similar modern gars and needlefish.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of bone boluses suggests that Saurichthys either attacked marine reptiles like Langobardisaurus or scavenged their remains.
facts.quote: Fossil evidence, in the form of a bolus (ball-shaped mass) of bones in the same strata, indicates that Saurichthys attacked marine reptiles such as the tanystropheid Langobardisaurus, or possibly scavenged their corpses.

facts.statement: Studies of the gastrointestinal tract reveal that Saurichthys had a spiral valve with many windings, similar to present-day sharks and rays.
facts.quote: A study on the gastrointestinal tract of Saurichthys found similarities with present-day sharks and rays, in particular the many windings in the spiral valve.

facts.statement: Fossils of pregnant females provide evidence that Saurichthys was viviparous, representing the oldest known example of this trait in ray-finned fishes.
facts.quote: Fossils of gravid females provide evidence for (ovo-)viviparity in Saurichthys and the oldest known example for viviparity in ray-finned fishes.

facts.statement: Specialized pelvic fin rays or ventral scales in certain species are interpreted as male copulatory organs, providing evidence for internal fertilization.
facts.quote: Internal fertilisation is also evidenced by specialized pelvic fin rays (Saurichthys calcaratus) or ventral scales (gonopodium; Saurichthys curionii, Saurichthys macrocephalus) that are interpreted as copulatory organs of males.

facts.statement: While historically classified as close relatives of sturgeons and paddlefish within Chondrostei, modern studies suggest Saurichthys may lie outside the Actinopterygii crown group.
facts.quote: Historically, they have been seen as close relatives of the Acipenseriformes (which includes living sturgeon and paddlefish) as part of the Chondrostei, though this has been strongly questioned by modern studies, which suggests that it may lie outside the Actinopterygii crown group.

facts.statement: Saurichthys is an extinct genus of prehistoric ray-finned fish belonging to the order Saurichthyiformes.
facts.quote: Saurichthys es un género extinto de peces actinopterigios prehistóricos del orden Saurichthyiformes.

facts.statement: The genus was scientifically described by Agassiz in 1843.
facts.quote: Este género marino fue descrito científicamente por Agassiz en 1843.

facts.statement: Saurichthys is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Actinopterygii, order Saurichthyiformes, and family Saurichthyidae.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Actinopterygii ordo: Saurichthyiformes familia: Saurichthyidae

facts.statement: Saurichthys fossils date from the Capitanian to the Bathonian, spanning 264.28 to 165.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Capitanian to Bathonian (264.28 to 165.3 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 239 recorded fossil occurrences of Saurichthys.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 239

facts.statement: Zhang et al. (2026) reported the first fossil evidence of Saurichthys in the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna in China.
facts.quote: Zhang et al. (2026) report the first fossil evidence of presence of Saurichthys in the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna (China).
